title: Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38)
hookLine: shown his own seal, Judah says "She is more righteous than I"

lines: THE STORY CUTS AWAY TO JUDAH.
SENT HOME TO WAIT, AND FORGOTTEN.
cards: Right in the middle of Joseph's story, just as he's dragged off to Egypt, the Torah cuts away, like a TV show that suddenly spends a whole episode on a side character. The side character is Judah.
His oldest son marries a woman named Tamar, and dies. By the custom of the time, the next son should give her a child in his brother's name. He refuses, and dies too.
Judah has one son left, and he's afraid. So he sends Tamar back to her father's house: wait until my youngest grows up. Then he never sends for her.
Tamar is left waiting, a widow with no future.

teach.b: Years pass. Tamar hears that Judah is coming through on the way to shear his sheep. She takes off her widow's clothes, covers her face with a veil, and sits by the road.
Judah doesn't recognize her; he thinks she's a woman for hire.

teach.h: A SEAL, A CORD, A STAFF.
teach.b: He has nothing to pay with, so she asks for a pledge: your seal, your cord, and your staff. His ID card, basically. Three months later, word comes: Tamar is pregnant.
Judah, the head of the family, gives the sentence: bring her out and let her be burned. As she's being brought out, Tamar sends a message. Not an accusation.
She doesn't say, it was you. She sends the seal, the cord and the staff: the man who owns these is the father.
Please look, whose are these? That word, look, recognize, is the same Hebrew the brothers used when they handed Jacob the bloody coat: look, is this your son's?
That time they asked their father to recognize a lie, and a midrash puts those words in Judah's mouth. Now Judah is asked to recognize something true.

teach.h: SHE IS MORE RIGHTEOUS THAN I.
teach.b: And he does: "She is more righteous than I." The Talmud notices how Tamar did it. She was ready to die rather than shame him in public; she gave him the chance to admit it himself.
Tamar has twins, Perez and Zerah.
And from Perez, the book of Ruth tells us, comes King David.

how: Jewish tradition draws from Tamar the teaching that publicly shaming another person is gravely wrong, and honors Judah's admission as a model of owning a mistake; Tamar's son Perez is remembered as an ancestor of King David.

o: here is my pledge, keep it safe
please forgive me, I was wrong

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: ready to die rather than shame him
she is more righteous than I

s: she sent his things with a question, whose are these? and let him admit it himself.
the Hebrew for look, recognize, also appears when the brothers show Jacob the coat
the same words tie the two stories together.
her son Perez is an ancestor of King David, the book of Ruth says.

games.q: you're Tamar, being led out to be burned. you hold the proof of who the father is: Judah's own seal, cord and staff. what do you do?
o: shout his name in front of everyone.
send him his things, and let him decide.
stay silent and accept the sentence.
games.why: she sends the items with a quiet question, whose are these? the Talmud says she'd rather die than shame him. Judah admits it: she is more righteous than I.

practice: Think of a disagreement, big or small, where you dug in and later realized the other person had it right; maybe you never told them. Picture saying Judah's words in your own way: you were right, and I was wrong.
Notice what that feels like in your chest, heavier or lighter.

wordCard.voice: Haker na, Hebrew for please recognize, look, the words that tie the bloody coat to Judah's own seal. She was wronged and left waiting; he judged her, then recognized his own seal and said she was the righteous one.

orig.note: Hebrew: please recognize, look. said to Jacob about the coat, and to Judah about his seal.

carryVoice: Your line: she was right. And Judah was the one who said it. Day sixty-seven is yours.

sources.q: She is more righteous than I
